description_program_dutch.nl:
Nanobiology studies the interaction of physics and biology and how these two fields are integrated in the study of fundamental medical research. It is a technical study that uses the languages and techniques of mathematics, physics and biology to understand what is happening inside a cell. 

During the bachelor you will develop an integrated understanding of mathematics, physics, and biology. You will study cell processes and learn how to model the behaviour of molecules. You will work with advanced microscopes and write computer programmes to do in-depth analysis and research. Nanobiologists use these skills to study diseases and processes such as cancer, Alzheimer’s, diabetes, neurological processing, and aging. The programme is intended to educate students to earn a Bachelor of Science degree in Nanobiology, providing them with such a level of knowledge, insight and skills in the area of Nanobiology, that graduates can fulfil positions on the labour market at the Bachelors level. It is a three year programme (180 ECs).

The programme consists of two years of required coursework (120 ECs) 2/3 of these courses are theory courses focused on developing knowledge in the fields of single cell biology, molecular imaging, computational modeling, biophysics. The other third is practical courses designed to develop skills in a variety of environments--wet lab, computational, instrumentation, professional. All courses include developing durable skills in critical thinking, collaboration and communication. Theory courses often include a practical or two, and practical courses require learning some theory.

In the third year offers students can explore. It consists of 30 EC space for a minor. This can be a structured minor at a Dutch university, an exchange programme, or self-composed set of courses, it does not need to be nanobiology related and we encourage students to explore areas of interest. There is also 10 EC of electives, where students can choose at least four 2.5 EC electives offered by the Nanobiology bachelor. Students complete an individual 20 EC Bachelor End Project which consists of lab work, data analysis, and working with an active research group at TU Delft or Erasmus MC.

Our programme is structured to provide students instruction and opportunities to master our Final Attainment Levels (FAL) which are described below. When students graduate they should be able to:

FAL.1.   Understand fundamental knowledge of Math, Physics and Biology in field of Nanobiology including reading scientific literature (Knowledge) 

FAL.2.   Use methods and techniques of Nanobiology research including computational biosciences and imaging (Methods and Techniques) 

FAL.3.    Conduct experiments in fields of molecular biology, biophysics, computational biosciences, imaging,  including troubleshooting (Practicals) 

FAL.4.    Design research questions and experiments (Design) 

FAL.5.   Collaborate effectively in international and interdisciplinary environments (Interdisciplinary) 

FAL.6.   Communicate scientific ideas and results in oral, visual and written forms (Communicate) 

FAL.7.   Critically discuss ethical concepts in the field of nanobiological research and relevance to society (Ethics) 

Education takes place at TU Delft campus and in the Erasmus MC in Rotterdam.

Schedule information can be found at MyTimetable - Timetable view | Delft University of Technology

courseEvidence.vakbeschrijving: In this course the student will learn the principles of genetics, ranging from classical Mendelian genetics to the most recent molecular genetics techniques. Both the theoretical and practical aspects of genetics will be taught, including DNA/RNA structure, gene function, genome organization, inheritance, DNA replication, repair and recombination and mutation. A major part of this course will cover various classical and modern molecular genetic techniques from the genomics era. The course includes individual and group exercises focusing on solving genetic problems. The knowledge gained in this course will show the student how to design and interpret genetic experiments, to answer relevant genetic questions. Students will need this knowledge for other courses.

courseEvidence.vakbeschrijving: In Math 1, we cover the mathematics to work towards three big topics: Differential equations, Taylor series and Line integrals. These topics will all come back in the Mechanics & Optics course (NB1325). Math 1 is divided in four blocks: Basics We cover some standard techniques on one variable functions, such as (inverse) trigonometric functions limits derivatives linearisation integration techniques such as substitution, integration by parts, partial fractions and improper integrals As a nanobiology student, you can expect these methods be used in Math 1, Math 2 and Math 3, but also many of your other courses. Differential equations In this block, you learn to solve some differential equations: Separable first order differential equations Linear first order differential equations Linear second order differential equations with constant coefficients. Along the way, we also cover complex numbers phase lines. You will revisit the second order differential equations in your Mechanics & Optics course (NB1325), in the context of mass spring systems. The section on complex numbers will also serve as a primer on polar coordinates, helpful to describe centripetal force. Series In this block, you will work towards the topic of Taylor series and their applications. They are used in your Mechanics & Optics course (NB1325), but also relevant for topics like Fourier series, and partitions in Introduction to Soft Matter. Along the way, we cover Basics of sequences and series Various methods to test for convergence: comparison test, alternating series test, ratio test Power series Taylor series Some error estimates Some applications Line integrals The standard use case for Line integrals is the computation of the physical concept Work. As ever, you will encounter this in your Mechanics & Optics course (NB1325). To explain line integrals, we will encounter Vectors, lines, planes and multivariate functions Partial derivatives and linearization Vector fields Integrating scalar fields Integrating vector fields Conservative vector fields
courseEvidence.leerdoelen: Students can compute limits, derivatives and integrals of univariate functions. Students can solve ordinary differential equations numerically, exactly and qualitatively. Students can perform computations with complex numbers. Students can compute and analyse series, including power series and Taylor series. Students can analyse multivariate functions using partial differentiation. Students can compute line integrals of scalar functions and vector fields.

courseEvidence.vakbeschrijving: Chemistry studies the composition, properties and transformations of matter. Understanding chemistry is especially important for research at the nanoscale, where complex interactions between molecules are governed by chemical forces and barriers. courseEvidence.vakbeschrijving: Classical mechanics is a core topic in all the natural sciences. Not only does it define what common words like "force", "momentum" and "energy" precisely mean in the sciences, it is also the discipline holding the secrets to creating stable constructions, describing the motion of moving objects and predicting where they will go, whether they are very large (stars, planets), a little smaller (bicycles, sail boats) or tiny (a swimming bacterium). It is an ancient discipline, practiced all around the globe, but formalised in Europe on a mathematical basis in the 17th century, where Newton's name ultimately became attached to it (and many others, like Gallilei, Stevin, Huijgens, etc.). Throughout history it has allowed societies to build fantastic structures, make use of wonderful vehicles and devices, including tools to destroy them again, with cannon balls and other projectiles. In the same century that the laws of mechanics were formulated in the way we know them today, a successful cloth retailer and local politician in Delft took an interest in lensmaking. Driven by a lively scientific spirit, Anthonie van Leeuwenhoek was able to design a microscope powerful enough to observe forms of life invisible to the human eye. With great wonder he described his observations of tiny creatures that he called "animalcules" or, in Dutch, "dierkens". For these discoveries he is currently credited as the "father of microbiology". In the final two weeks of the course, the secrets to building a (modern) microscope will be revealed. Techniques from "ray optics" are used to predict the location of the images of lenses and curved mirrors. Other phenomena of light, such as reflection, refraction, diffraction, interference are also discussed in detail. While learning the academic approach In this course, you will recognise some topics that were essential to the physics classes in highschool, but are now presented in a more formal, abstract way, with much more rigorous mathematical language, which will ultimately allow you to tackle much more complex questions that you might encounter in the lab, or in everyday life. These topics will be illustrated by exciting, well-designed experiments, demonstrated in class, connecting the abstract equations to beautiful phenomena, and showing their power. The abstract, academic approach will allow you to see that all the topics are intimately connected to each other, and that they follow from only a few principles. This is different from the more conceptual highschool approach, where there seem to be separate laws for each situation. To see the connections between concepts, it is necessary to go through mathematical derivations, linking one relation to the next. In the end, this process will create a cohesive, comprehensive understanding of the laws of physics, and an ability to use these laws confidently and creatively. Ultimately, once these connections are understood and integrated, it will give the experience that physics is actually "really easy", and equip that person with an intuition where they can "feel" a solution, or the road towards it. This skill is essential in the lab, where researchers have to work on projects that do not have a solution manual, and where they have to find a road in the dark themselves, using a systematic approach and a good amount of intuition. However, as long as the topics are not mastered, a person may experience the exact opposite, that physics is "very difficult". In that case, know that mastery comes with practice. The course provides ample opportunity for practice, in a whole spectrum of ways. During the course there will be interactive live lectures that introduce the relevant concepts, and work sessions with a library of practice materials on a Grasple platform. This platform can be used to gradually practice towards mastery with exercise sets for every lecture. A group assignment will stimulate collaboration and communication skills.

courseEvidence.vakbeschrijving: Nanobiology focuses on studying biology at the nanoscale. Experiments in this field of science often generate large datasets that require complex analyses. To make sense of all this data, researchers rely on (the quality of) computational tools and software they often write themselves. In this course you will build the foundations in computational thinking, a fundamental programming competence. You will learn to write Python programs, and use tools such as Git for version control, VS Code and command line. You will go beyond simply using these tools - you will develop a systematic approach to solving problems by using techniques such as chunking (breaking problems into smaller parts), debugging, and responsible use of AI. No prior knowledge is needed to follow this course. Different learning paths and exercises at various levels are provided, allowing you to build your own toolbox with Python functions, programming concepts, and problem-solving strategies. You’ll progress from learning the basics of programming syntax to analyzing nanobiology-relevant data, creating informative visualizations, and ultimately build your own biomolecular simulation which can be used to explore the influence of relevant parameters on the biological system, and may even inspire new research directions.
courseEvidence.leerdoelen: At the end of the course the student is able to: 1. Recognize basic concepts in working with computers and programming. 2. Effectively use programming software and supporting applications, in particular a computer terminal, an integrated development environment, and Git. 3. Use variables, functions, conditions, flow control, data files, and plotting to create Python code that addresses nanobiology problems. 4. Recognize and correct errors in Python code. 5. Apply style guidelines for code readability when writing Python code. 6. Review code created by others, improve it and provide useful feedback. 7. Combine the above skills to implement algorithms that simulate movement and diffusion of biomolecules within and between compartments and the interaction of individual molecules with each other. 8. Demonstrate understanding of biomolecular dynamic equilibria and steady state systems.

courseEvidence.toetsing: NB1420 is a practical course. For the assessments, one of the two trajectories must be chosen in the first week of the course. It is designed for those who have no prior experience or do not feel confident with programming. In trajectory I, the final grade will be composed of: - 60 % assignments, each of the three assignments counts for 20 % of the grade - 10 % "staying on track" activities - 30 % final project --------------- Trajectory II "Experienced programmer": This trajectory is designed for those who feel confident with programming. Taking part in the "staying on track" activities is still recommended but is not obligatory. In trajectory II, the final grade will be composed of: - 70 % assignments, each counts 23.3% of the grade, participating in "staying on track" activities is optional and does not contribute to the final grade - 30 % final project Assignments There will be 3 graded assignments completed in class. Students will have one opportunity to redo 1 or 2 assignments in week 2.9 (repair session). - Students will not be able to repair all three assignments. - Missing an assignment during class will limit a student’s opportunities for repairing the results on other assignments, since they will need to do the one they missed during the repair session. - Students must enroll for the repair session via BrightSpace, before week 2.9. The exact deadline will be communicated by teachers. - If a student attempts an assignment more than once, the best grade will be used in final grade calculations. - Being present at the assignment session (i.e., signing the presence sheet) counts as an attempt. The full details of the activities and the time schedule will be announced in the beginning of the course, and made available on Brightspace. There are no repair options for staying on track activities. If a student in Trajectory I doesn't take part in any of the staying on track activities, they can still pass the course with the grade of 9. courseEvidence.vakbeschrijving: This course represents the interface between chemistry and biology and studies life at a molecular level. Our knowledge about the molecular composition of cells and the complex network of chemical reactions that take place within them is expanding rapidly. In this course you will study the molecular composition of cells and the major metabolic pathways involved, with special emphasis will on the structure and function of enzymes and bioenergetics. This course also teaches the basic determinants and elements of biomolecular structure and dynamics, structure-function relations, and current methods in structure determination, with a focus on proteins and their complexes with other biomolecules. It furthermore provides practical information on how to navigate the publicly available structural databases and how to interpret, analyze and optimally visualize biomolecular structures.
courseEvidence.leerdoelen: At the completion of this course, the students will be able to: 1. Describe and recognize the major molecular constituents of the cell, their function and how they are synthesized from precursors. 2. Qualitatively and quantitatively describe energetic principles that define biomolecular structure and function and the effect of mutations. 3. Calculate the rate of enzymatic reactions and predict how this rate is affected by activators, inhibitors and specific mutations. 4. Explain how metabolic pathways are regulated to maintain homeostasis. 5. Describe photosynthesis, how mitochondria convert the energy that is stored in reduction equivalents into ATP and how the ATD/ADP ratio regulates cellular metabolism 6. Have insight into current methods for macromolecular structure determination 7. Be able to analyze experimentally and computationally determined biomolecular structures

courseEvidence.vakbeschrijving: In this course you will learn the basics of linear algebra. In linear algebra you will study high-dimensional mathematics, in particular involving vectors and matrices. This course focuses on properties of systems of linear equations, linear transformations, linear subspaces and dimensions and determinants. In the second part of this course we continue the study of calculus with a focus on 2 and 3 dimensions. In particular we will start with some topics in high-dimensional differentiation (directional derivatives, implicit differentiation, Taylor polynomials, curvature). Subsequently we will consider integrals over 2 and 3 dimensional domains (including in polar, cylindrical and spherical coordinates).
courseEvidence.leerdoelen: After completion of this course, students should be able to Analyse the properties of various concepts in linear algebra using row reduction. Apply the basic operations of matrices and vectors. Analyse the properties of linear subspaces. Express themselves correctly in the language of linear algebra to explain their arguments. Compute and use directional derivatives, gradients and perform implicit differentiation for multivariate functions. Compute multivariate integrals in 2D and 3D, including changing to familiar and new coordinate systems. Rewrite select physical properties to integrals.

courseEvidence.vakbeschrijving: This course introduces students to the physical principles governing biological processes at the molecular and cellular scale. It covers thermodynamics, continuum mechanics, stochastic processes, and statistical mechanics in a biophysical context. Topics include temperature, heat and work, entropy, fluid flow, elasticity, diffusion, random walks, low-Reynolds-number motion, biopolymer mechanics, and self-assembly. Students apply concepts from earlier courses--especially Mechanics and Optics, Biochemistry & Structural Biology and Chemistry--and use Python to model and analyse biophysical systems. The course emphasizes how quantitative physical approaches can be used to understand biological function, organisation, and dynamics.
courseEvidence.leerdoelen: After completion of this course, students should be able to: explain how physical laws apply to biological phenomena across molecular and cellular length scales apply core concepts from thermal physics, including temperature, heat and work, the first and second laws of thermodynamics, and entropy, to biophysical systems analyse continuum-mechanics problems relevant to biology, including fluid flow, viscosity, pressure, elasticity, and beam bending describe and model stochastic processes in biology, including random walks, diffusion, drag, and low-Reynolds-number motion quantitatively analyse the conformations, mechanics, and entropic elasticity of biopolymers use concepts from statistical mechanics, including microstates, Boltzmann distributions, free energy, and chemical potential, to explain molecular self-assembly and molecular recognition use analytical methods and Python-based simulations to study and interpret biophysical systems connect physical models to biological examples, experiments, and literature in molecular and cellular biophysics.

courseEvidence.vakbeschrijving: We begin this course with vector calculus; the study of integrals over curves and surfaces in 2 and 3 dimensions. In particular you will learn about the theorems of Green, Gauss, and Stokes. Next you will study some more advanced concepts of linear algebra. We start with eigenvalues of a matrix, which provides better insight in what happens if you multiply a vector by that matrix. Next we consider the effects of orthogonality ("perpendicularness"), which amongst other things leads to regression (how best to draw a straight line through a set of experimental data). Finally we combine the two in the study of symmetric matrices which allow us to analyze quadratic forms and decompose a matrix in its singular value decompositions. The course ends with the study of maxima and minima of functions of several variables (which uses the quadratic forms you just learned about), both local and global. In this topic you will also learn the technique of Lagrange multipliers.
courseEvidence.leerdoelen: Upon completion of this course students will be able to: Compute integrals and derivatives in the realm of vector calculus. Analyse a matrix or linear transformation based on its eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Perform computations related to orthogonality. Analyse symmetric matrices and related concepts using orthogonal diagonalization and singular value decomposition. Apply linear algebra in applications like discrete dynamical systems and linear regression. Express themselves fluently in the language of linear algebra to explain their arguments. Compute (local and global) extreme values of multivariate functions.

courseEvidence.vakbeschrijving: In Electricity and Magnetism we continue the exploration of classical physics from the first year course Mechanics and Optics . The course gives an introduction to the empirical laws of electromagnetism and will allow you to understand basic circuit components resistors, capacitors and inductors, as well as the electromagnetic wave equation and special relativity. You will learn the theory behind these elements and concepts, and how to apply the theory to practical examples. In the lectures we will focus on the theory and we will work through examples together. In the exercise classes after each days lecture you will practice applying the theory with the help of TA's and the exercise platform Grasple. We will also do a few simulation exercises allowing you to build virtual circuits and test things out in practice (digitally).
courseEvidence.leerdoelen: 1. Explain and use the empirical laws of electrostatics to calculate electric forces, fields and potentials. 2. Explain and use the empirical laws of magnetism to calculate magnetic forces and fields. 3. Explain the connection between the Maxwell Equation and the empirical laws of electromagnetism. 4. Explain and apply basic concepts in Special Relativity. 5. Apply the laws of electromagnetism to explain and analyse the action of standard circuit elements (resistor, capacitor, and inductor). 6. courseEvidence.vakbeschrijving: Science, Technology and Society I introduces students to the societal and ethical questions raised by new and emerging sciences and technologies (NESTs), with specific attention to nanobiology. The course is the first in a two-course, full-year trajectory that examines how emerging technologies generate societal questions, hopes, fears, and ethical concerns, how these responses shape the development and governance of nanobiological science and technology, and what roles nanobiology professionals can assume in a dynamic interplay of science, technology and society. Part 1: Imaginaries of emerging technologies The first part of the course focuses on the ways in which NESTs are imagined by experts, stakeholders and general publics. Emerging technologies often give rise to utopian and dystopian future scenarios, ranging from promises of medical progress and human enhancement to fears about risk, inequality, surveillance, or loss of control. Students examine how these imaginaries express (normative) assumptions about science, society, responsibility, and desirable futures. Part 2: Ethics and regulation The second part of the course focuses on how societies respond to the ethical and societal questions raised by nanobiological NESTs. Students examine how ethical reflection, legal frameworks, professional standards, and national and international regulation help assess and govern nanobiological research and technology. This part shows that NESTs do not develop in isolation, but are shaped by social, ethical, legal, and institutional contexts.
courseEvidence.leerdoelen: Explain why new and emerging sciences and technologies (NESTs) generate societal questions, hopes, fears, and ethical concerns. Analyze utopian and dystopian imaginaries of NESTs and identify the assumptions, values, and forms of technological “magical thinking” they express. Analyze ethical and societal concerns raised by nanobiological NESTs by distinguishing relevant actors, interests, risks, responsibilities, and possible consequences. Apply relevant ethical, legal, professional, national, and international regulatory frameworks to concrete cases in nanobiological research and technology. Collaboratively communicate the results of an ethical or regulatory analysis of a nanobiological NEST.

courseEvidence.vakbeschrijving: All animal species develop from a single cell, the fertilized egg, and share genes which regulate development. A large number of genes encoding components of molecular and cellular mechanisms involved in development are highly conserved among animal species. Yet, nature shows us an astonishing variety of animal forms. The basis for this variety lies in genome diversification through mechanisms such as gene duplication and mutation events, which generate opportunities for further modification and refinement of developmental schemes, resulting in new forms and functions, if the new phenotypes are successful under natural selection. Evolution and diversification of animal forms occurs through changes in development. By studying developmental biology in an evolutionary context, we gain a much better understanding of the mechanisms at work in animal development. In this course, the students will learn about general aspects of development across the animal kingdom: from worms and flies to fish, birds, and mammals. It goes without saying that this approach also provides an illuminating picture of our own development.
courseEvidence.leerdoelen: Upon completion of this course, the student will be able to: 1. Describe evolutionary conserved concepts of animal development and cell differentiation in various model species (Understand) 2. Identify embryo stages and key structures at different phases in different model organisms (Remember) 3. Explain similarities and differences between different model species at the level of gene regulation, cells, embryo structures, organs and limbs; using knowledge on the biological processes that are at the base of those similarities and differences. (Understand) 4. Describe the basic evolutionary concepts about the development of multicellularity, sexual reproduction, and Darwins theories concerning speciation (Understand) 5. Connect specific evolutionary events to the appropriate evolutionary concept. (Apply) 6. Provide the definitions of toti- and pluripotency of cells (Remember) 7. Assess the possibilities of the use of different types of (induced) pluri- and totipotent stem cells in research and therapeutic applications (Evaluate) 8. Critically interpret the results of scientific experiments in developmental biology, using provided text and figures from scientific manuscripts. (Analyse) 9. Develop a research question using information gained from a scientific literature search (Create) 10. courseEvidence.vakbeschrijving: In the 1990's a large and diverse community of scientists and researchers from the industry, who were driven together by common interests, united and identified their activities under the name "Soft Matter". The interests of this community all related to the properties of matter, and techniques to interrogate, understand, and change these properties, often with the goal of designing new materials with desirable properties. Soft Matter offered a common ground for physicists, chemists, computational scientists, biologists, and industrial researchers interested in food, medicine, advanced materials, energy storage, oil recovery, and a wide spectrum of other applications. The word "Soft" refers to the interactions between the components of the material at the microscale. Complicated materials, and in particular biological materials, are formed via a process called self-assembly, or self-organisation, and this process can only take place if the interactions between the components are 'soft', i.e. easily disturbed by thermal fluctuations or other sources of energy input. In biology, the typical interaction strength between proteins or e.g. the base pairs of DNA, is of the order of the thermal energy. Such an interaction is strong enough to withstand thermal noise, for some time, and form complex structures, but weak enough to reorganise, and be dynamically regulated by the cell, or some external stimulus. This being said, Soft Matter is hard: the experimental and theoretical techniques are sophisticated, and systems can be very complex. Also literally, some 'soft materials' are very robust, and difficult to deform. The course: Introduction to Soft Matter This course will provide an introduction to Soft Matter, and combines an overview of modern materials research, with fundamental techniques to interrogate, modify, and design these materials. In particular, this includes the study of biomolecular condensates, their physical properties and function. The first half of the course introduces the principles of Statistical Thermodynamics. After a quick review of probability theory and Classical Thermodynamics, the laws of thermodynamics are reformulated using Boltzmann's definition of entropy, and Statistical Mechanics. This theory couples the microscopic mechanics of molecules, to the macroscopic properties of the entire system. Important concepts are: Emergence, micro- and macrostates, Boltzmann entropy, thermodynamic ensembles, Boltzmann distribution, partition functions, correlation functions. The second half of the course will focus more on applications and phenomena at the nanoscale in cells. There will be questions why polymers are elastic, and what their spring constant is, why adding salt to a recipe may influence the cooking process, what a critical point is, and what the potential driving mechanisms are behind the self-organisation of proteins into temporal membrane-less organelles. These questions will be answered. The property of systems to spontaneously organise, or undergo phase transitions, will be explored in detail, and ultimately be related to the properties of the components of the system. Reaction-diffusion systems, Turing mechanisms, and Information Theory will conclude the course. In a final group project, this knowledge needs to be applied, with a good amount of creativity, to discover design rules for a Soft Matter system, via an experiment in silico (a computer simulation) or in the kitchen (the results have to be edible and healthy), or both.
courseEvidence.leerdoelen: After successful completion of the course, students should be able to 1. Understand the concepts and principles of Statistical Thermodynamics 2. Identify physical mechanisms driving biological systems, with Soft Matter skills. 4. Apply the basic principles of Information Theory to embryonal development and sensing. 5. Conduct a research project in a small group, to discover design principles for a Soft Matter system. 6. courseEvidence.vakbeschrijving: Microscopy images contain a wealth of information. Extracting this information in a way that is not subject to error requires 1) understanding the physics of image formation to assess the limits of physical information present; 2) using mathematical concepts underlying digital image formation and analysis to allow for objective and complete information extraction; 3) comparing different microscopy methods to assess what method should be used to obtain a specific type of information and 4) the ability to automate image analysis tasks by using a computer and appropriate methods to efficiently, accurately and reproducibly extract objective, complete and physically relevant information. In this course the student will apply the knowledge obtained in Imaging 1 in practice. The student will learn to analyse complex imaging data from relevant papers, and perform experiments involving advanced microscopy concepts. The student will be introduced to advanced imaging and image analysis concepts, among others Single molecule localization Microscopy (SMLM), Total internal reflection (TIRF), Structured Illumination microscopy (SIM), fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), tracking, registration, data visualization and neural networks. These advanced concepts, as well as the basic concepts from imaging 1, will be brought into practice as the student will be guided through current fluorescence microscopy techniques for quantitatively studying cellular function and dysfunction at the nanoscopic scale. The students will work (in groups of five) on various topics (four will be chosen from a total of six) using different advanced fluorescence bioimaging techniques: cell division (mitosis and meiosis) will be studied using confocal time lapse microscopy and single molecule localisation (SMLM) (topics 1, 2), the assembly of microtubules will be studied using total internal reflection (TIRF) microscopy and the role of focal adhesions in migration using structured illumination microscopy (SIM) (topics 3, 4), gene transcription regulation will be studied by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) (topic 5), cell membranes will be visualised and cell volume/surface ratios will be determined using specific membrane and nuclear staining and 3-D confocal microscopy (topic 6). For each topic the students use the various state-of-the-art research microscopes to record images (under supervision), analyse the data, write a report and in a final session discuss the reports with the supervisor in a 15 minute session. Topics not covered in the practical sessions are explored by reviewing relevant papers, where students use the advanced concepts introduced to extract relevant info and discuss the paper and its methodologies. The course is closely related to all Nanobiology courses as a variety of cell biological model systems are investigated using microscopes, analysed using mathematical techniques and reported in writing and discussed afterwards.

courseEvidence.vakbeschrijving: Science, Technology and Society II builds on Science, Technology and Society I, and is the second of a two-course, full-year trajectory that examines how emerging technologies generate societal questions, hopes, fears, and ethical concerns, and how these concerns can be understood and addressed. Where STS I examines how NESTs generate hopes, fears, and societal responses, STS II shifts attention to science itself as a socially organized way of responding to uncertainty, and to the moral responsibilities of future nanobiology professionals. Part 1: Science, evidence and public trust The first part of the course focuses on science as a social institution for producing reliable knowledge. Students examine how scientific claims are supported, challenged, and made trustworthy through organized skepticism, peer criticism, diverse evidence standards, and public communication. They also analyze how scientific claims become credible or contested in public debate, especially in relation to controversial health-related claims. Part 2: Stakeholder engagement and professional responsibility The second part of the course focuses on the moral responsibilities of future nanobiology professionals. Students examine and practice stakeholder engagement around ethical and societal issues in nanobiology and reflect on their own (future) professional identity, moral responsibilities, values and virtues. This part concludes the STS trajectory by moving from collective societal and institutional responses to questions of individual responsibility and ethical deliberation in professional practice.
courseEvidence.leerdoelen: Analyze how science is socially organized to produce reliable knowledge through organized skepticism, diverse evidence standards, and public trust. Evaluate controversial health-related scientific claims by comparing different types of evidence, identifying selective use of evidence, and assessing the role of scientific consensus. Explain how scientific claims become credible or contested in public debate, including the role of uncertainty, communication, and different interpretations of evidence. Design and reflect on stakeholder engagement around ethical and societal issues in nanobiology. Develop and critically reflect on one’s own professional identity, moral responsibilities, values, virtues, and ability to deliberate on ethical dilemmas as a future nanobiology professional.

courseEvidence.vakbeschrijving: Context of the course Our increasing understanding of diseases like cancer has led to new drugs becoming available for clinical application. While the application of these new drugs leads to increased cure rates, their high cost and potential side effects also pose a pressure on health care cost for society and individual patient outcomes. In the era of personalized medicine, we aim to provide drugs only to patients benefitting from them. Genomics techniques help us to better position new and current treatments, yielding biomarkers discriminating patients sensitive from refractory to treatment. Furthermore, the basic knowledge gained through genomics research allows for new treatments to be developed further improving patient care. Aims of the course This course highlights state-of-the-art technological developments in the fields of genomics and how these tools can be applied to discover new biomarkers and what we learn from their use with regard to the understanding of mechanisms of disease progression. Breast cancer, a common cancer in humans, is used as an example. The course specifically aims to provide an understanding of normal mammary gland development and how breast cancer can arise in epithelial cells from the mammary gland due to hereditary as well as somatically acquired mutational programs. Furthermore, it is discussed how this knowledge can used to optimize patient care allowing for patient stratification involving both predictive and prognostic markers and for monitoring disease using innovative diagnostic tools. Teaching activities: The course will be given in the format of classical lectures and will cover an introduction of breast cancer pathology, physiology and molecular biology. Also the genetics of the disease will be reviewed. Different types of technological platforms for genomics research will be reviewed as well as to some details the bioinformatics and mathematics behind the applied data analysis tools. The course also includes a journal club in which the students will present and discuss literature related to the topics and learning objectives of this course. Overall, during the course, students will get a clearer understanding of how technology and the mathematics behind it can be applied to relevant issues in the field of cancer research and aid in understanding disease progression and therapy resistance. During the lectures, students understanding of the matter will be actively tested. During a journal club, students will read assigned literature and prepare a presentation and propose discussion points for their peers. This course is essential to understand the mechanisms of disease progression which helps the develop new treatment on the one hand but also can help in keeping cancer treatment cost effective. Students are expected to read the background literature provided as well actively participating to the lectures by posing questions. Furthermore, a critical attitude is expected when selected scientific literature related to the topics of the course is being prepared for during the journal club. At any moment during the course I am available for questions by email and will reply within 24 hours. During the preparation of the presentation for the journal club I will be present on site.
courseEvidence.leerdoelen: Learning objectives of the course NB3020: After this course the students should be able to: 1. Describe the cell types essential for normal mammary development as well as the cell types from which breast cancer can arise Success criteria: Student will be able to describe the anatomy including the hierarchy of the different cell types of the mammary gland. Furthermore, the student will be able to describe the pathology of breast cancer including the different stages of disease progression. 2. State the difference between driver and passenger mutations (understand) Success criterion: Student is able to explain why certain mutations cause cancer and others not. 3. Differentiate between prognostic and predictive markers (analyze) Success criteria: Student is able to explain the clinical management of breast cancer and how prognostic and predictive markers are applied in the clinical setting. 4. Describe the key features of the three dominant mutational program in breast cancer and their clinical significance (understand) Success criteria: Students have understood why mutations arise in breast cancer and if and how this can be clinically exploited 5. Differentiate between low, intermediate and high risk genes/alleles for getting breast cancer and methods to detect them most efficiently Success criteria: Students understand the complexity of hereditary breast cancer and able to apply this for the benefit of the patient 6. Differentiate between intra- and inter-tumor heterogeneity Success criteria: Students are able to understand how cancers evolve and why this is relevant for therapy failure 7. Describe methods to detect biomarkers in body fluid (i.e. liquid biopsies) Success criteria: Students are able to list various methods and can apply them in the appropriate setting Learn how to judge scientific literature, extract and summarize relevant information and present it to fellow-students (group effort) Success criteria: Students should be able to explain relevant content of a selected research article

courseEvidence.vakbeschrijving: This course provides an introduction into the field of complex genetics. Also referred to as population genetics; generating large-scale genetic datasets and then answering relevant biological or clinical questions. The course is split in four contact days and and exam: Day 1: Introduction to complex genetics and genome-wide association studies (genetic variation, genome-wide association studies - GWAS, applications of complex genetics). Day 2: Biological interpretation of GWAS results (functional interpretation of genetic variants, gene regulation). Day 3: Clinical application of GWAS results (disease risk prediction, polygenic risk scores, clinical decision-making) and future directions in the field. Day 4: Discussion of assignments; practical examples performed in groups or extracted from literature. Through these topics the course covers the basics of performing complex genetic studies, as well as some of the most common and currently utilized applications.

courseEvidence.vakbeschrijving: Introduction: many physical phenomena can be described by differential equations. In the context of Nanobiology you can think of processes like heat dispersion, diffusion or chemical reactions. Often these equations have to be solved numerically. First, the course will discuss how a system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) can be solved using numerical time integration. Then we discuss how a stationary diffusion equation can be discretized with the Finite Difference Method. Finally, we combine time integration and space discretization to numerically solve the heat equation. The theory will be explained in 4 sessions as described below: Lecture 1: Numerical integration and some time integration methods: Forward Euler, Backward Euler, Trapezoidal Method, Modified Euler. Implicit methods and Explicit methods. Predictor-corrector methods. Lecture 2: Stability of time integration methods, order of accuracy and systems of ordinary differential equations (ODEs). Lecture 3: Numerical differentiation and Finite Difference Method(s). Discretization of boundary conditions and properties of the discretization matrix. Lecture 4: Finite Difference Method (continued): (Non-constant) diffusion and the heat equation. The method of lines. After every lecture, there is a practical session where students should be present in class to: practice with the theory discussed during lectures using pen-and-paper exercises and Python implementations; use Python to numerically solve given problems; explain their Python code, implementation choices, and pen-and-paper solutions to the present instructors and/or teaching assistants in order to receive feedback; prepare for the final assignment, which will be an oral exam. Remark: whenever you choose not to be present in class, there are no possibilities to get extra explanation or feedback regarding the content of the lectures nor the practical sessions. This also includes the Python code and pen-and-paper exercises.
courseEvidence.leerdoelen: General: Given an initial value problem or boundary value problem, the student can make a motivated choice of appropriate numerical method to find a numerical approximation of the solution, and analyse the quality of the approximation. More specifically: The student knows, can successfully apply and can implement numerical time integration methods to solve ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and initial value problems, such as Forward Euler, Backward Euler, Trapezoidal Method, and Modified Euler. The student correctly classifies methods as implicit, explicit and/or predictor-corrector method, and can analyse strengths and weaknesses. The student correctly analyses stability and order of accuracy of time integration methods for (systems of) ODE(s). The student correctly applies, implements and analyses the discretisation of a given diffusion equation with the Finite Difference Method. The student correctly numerically solves the time-dependent heat equation with the method of lines. The student can clearly explain and justify all submitted work, implementation choices, and can provide detailed elaboration on stability analysis and accuracy of all methods used during practical sessions and in the final exam.

evidence.vakbeschrijving: How can our bodies have hundreds of different cell types, each having very different patterns of gene expression and well-defined behaviours and functions, and yet all have the same genome? Why do the cells in your skin divide into two other skin cells but not into two neurons or two muscle cells? How is it possible that our diets will affect our children and even grandchildren? All these facts have something in common which is the heritability of information across cell generations, without modifications to the DNA sequence. The field that studies this is Epigenetics. In this course, the students will deepen their understanding of the epigenetic mechanisms that mediate gene expression changes, development and disease. The course will be divided into three parts: 1. The first part will be devoted to describing what the different epigenetic mechanisms are, such as histone modifications and DNA methylation, that regulate genes in general, but also at the level of two paradigms in epigenetics, imprinted genes and X chromosome inactivation. We will also highlight the role of nuclear organization in gene expression control. 2. In the second part of this course, we will study how epigenetics affect development and disease, and we will look into epigenetic modulators that are used to combat disease. We will also discuss prions as a non-traditional epigenetic mechanism that can lead to disease. 3. Lastly, the students will learn what the different techniques are that are currently available to study epigenetic modifications and their implications, from basic biology to the medical field. This elective course is very relevant to Nanobiologists who want to expand their knowledge of epigenetic control of gene expression, how epigenetics is critical to understanding cell differentiation and development, and some types of diseases and cancer progression, and what the current technologies are used to study epigenetics in basic biology, medical research and biotechnological companies.
evidence.leerdoelen: At the completion of this course, the student will be able to: 1. Rephrase what epigenetics is. 2. Cite and explain the different types of epigenetic modifications that exist in mammals and what their mechanisms of action are in regulating gene expression. 3. Describe what imprinted genes and X chromosome inactivation are. 4. Explain how epigenetics can modulate disease and cancer progression. 5. Cite and explain the existing current technologies to study epigenetic mechanisms of gene expression control. 6. Rephrase essential concepts of epigenetics 7. Apply the obtained knowledge in order to critically describe, interpret and explain the results of scientific experiments in epigenetics, using provided text and figures from scientific manuscripts. 8. Read and critically assess scientific literature in the field of epigenetics. 9. Collaborate with fellow students to prepare a scientific presentation on an epigenetics topics. 10. Present a scientific argument, engage in discussion with fellow students and answer questions in public about epigenetics research. 11. Give peer feedback of presentations.
